title: How Face Transplants Work
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss face transplants, starting with the chimp attack in Connecticut and the history of transplantation from Joseph Murray's identical-twin kidney transplant through immunosuppressive drugs like cyclosporine and the rise of hand and heart transplants. They recount the 1994-style case of a nine-year-old Indian girl whose face and scalp were torn off in a threshing machine and reattached, then the 2005 case of Isabelle Dinoire (spelled Isabelle Dean Noir in transcript) whose lower face was damaged while she slept, the first major face transplant. They cover how donor faces are removed and matched (HLA/antigen testing), the Chinese bear-mauling partial transplant in 2006, the team sizes and surgery durations, the lifelong immunosuppressant drawbacks, a Chicago full face transplant and a Frenchman with elephant man disease in 2008, and ethical concerns about cosmetic use. The episode closes with plugs, listener mail about retiring Haiku Theater, and corrections about lava flows and magnetic north.
topics: Stuff You Should Know listener mail

segments.title: Opening banter and chimp attack
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter, then introduce face transplants by way of the chimp attack on a woman in Connecticut, which prompted talk of a possible face transplant for her.

segments.title: History of transplants and immune rejection
segments.summary: Joseph Murray performed the first successful kidney transplant using identical twins. The hosts explain that the body rejects foreign tissue, and that antigens trigger the immune response. Immunosuppressive drugs such as cyclosporine, developed by the 1960s, made transplants succeed, at the cost of susceptibility to infections.

segments.title: Progression to hand, heart and facial transplants
segments.summary: Heart transplants were mastered in the 1980s and 1990s, followed by hand transplants. The hosts note about fifty years passed between the first kidney transplant and the first face transplant.

segments.title: Indian girl's face reattached after threshing machine accident
segments.summary: A nine-year-old girl in northern India had her face, scalp and hair torn off in a threshing machine while chopping grass. Her family brought her to a hospital three hours away on a moped, and doctors reattached her face and scalp, which functioned afterward.

segments.title: Isabelle Dinoire's 2005 face transplant
segments.summary: Isabelle Dinoire, a Frenchwoman, woke after taking sleeping pills to find the lower half of her face gone, reportedly damaged while her black lab was with her. The hosts discuss conflicting accounts, including suicide attempt theories. She received the first major face transplant in 2005, with a donor face and the goal of restoring feeling and function. Surgery took a team of about fifty doctors over roughly eighteen hours.

segments.title: Donor requirements, matching, and surgical process
segments.summary: Face donors must be brain dead on life support with family consent, so the face is removed from a live donor and transported on ice. Surgeons match skin tone and antigens through HLA testing. Partial transplants include a 2006 case in China after a bear mauling, with teams of fifteen to twenty doctors. Surgeons practice on rats, cadavers and rabbits, and multiple surgeries are often needed. Recipients must take immunosuppressants for life, which raises health risks.

segments.title: Full face transplants and ethics
segments.summary: The hosts mention a full face transplant in Chicago performed at the Cleveland Clinic, and a Frenchman with elephant man disease who received new lips, cheeks, nose and mouth in March 2008. They discuss ethical concerns about cosmetic use and wealthy patients, and the possible future of face transplants.

segments.title: Plugs and listener mail
segments.summary: Plugs for the Stuff You Should Know blog and the Super Stuff Guide to the Economy. Listener mail retires the Haiku Theater segment and corrects an earlier episode on lava flows and magnetic north.
